title: IX. Integration and Conclusion

html:
The preceding sections have described a suite of social-cognitive systems–mentalizing, empathy, self-modeling, attachment, belonging, status, norms, and communication–that are often studied independently but are best understood as components of a single integrated architecture organized by the three superordinate objectives introduced in the theoretical framework: compression (building efficient generative models of self and others), empowerment (maximizing the agent’s causal influence over social outcomes), and expected free energy minimization (keeping the organism within its social viability envelope). Every system described here serves at least two of these objectives simultaneously, and their neural implementations share overlapping substrates precisely because they draw on common computational primitives–prediction error computation, precision weighting, recursive generative modeling, and homeostatic-style regulation over social variables.

The Architecture in Summary

The core architectural claim is that evolution has installed a layered social generative model whose structure reflects the computational demands of human ultra-sociality:

Layer 1 – Social perception (STS, FFA, voice-selective cortex, biological motion areas): rapid extraction of social signals from faces, voices, bodies, and gaze, providing the sensory likelihood terms that drive all downstream inference.

Layer 2 – Agent modeling (mentalizing network: TPJ, dmPFC, temporal poles; mirror/simulation circuits): constructing generative models of other agents’ beliefs, desires, intentions, traits, and likely actions–the computational engine for prediction in a world populated by intentional beings.

Layer 3 – Self-modeling (cortical midline structures, DMN, hippocampal–mPFC circuits): the reflexive application of agent-modeling to oneself, producing the identity representation that compresses one’s own behavioral complexity and signals predictability to social partners.

Layer 4 – Relational regulation (OT/opioid bonding circuits, mPFC–amygdala regulatory pathways, social pain/reward networks): maintaining the dyadic bonds (attachment) and group memberships (belonging) that constitute the social viability envelope, with dedicated neurochemical systems (oxytocin, μ\mu-opioid, serotonin) that convert social variables into homeostatic-format signals.

Layer 5 – Social structure tracking (striatal status-reward circuits, norm-enforcement networks in AI/dACC/DLPFC, fairness computation in vmPFC): monitoring and navigating the hierarchical and normative structure of the social environment – who has power, what rules apply, whether exchanges are fair.

Layer 6 – Communicative interface (perisylvian language network interfaced with mentalizing and person-knowledge systems): the high-bandwidth channel that enables propositional exchange, gossip-based reputation tracking, norm transmission, and narrative identity construction–amplifying every lower layer’s reach and precision.

These layers are not independent modules but form a deeply interactive hierarchy: social perception feeds agent modeling, which feeds self-modeling (via reflected appraisal), which feeds relational regulation (via IWM-based expectations), which feeds social-structure navigation (via status and norm computations calibrated by attachment security and belonging state), which feeds communication (whose pragmatic content presupposes all lower layers). Disruption at any layer cascades upward and downward–explaining why social-cognitive deficits rarely present in isolation, and why conditions affecting early layers (e.g., autism spectrum: atypical social perception and mentalizing) produce pervasive downstream consequences across the entire social-cognitive architecture. Source maps compare default-mode and social-cognition networks (Figure) 1. A complementary network diagram connects mirroring and mentalizing systems (Figure) 2.

Evolutionary Priors vs. Learned Content

A recurring theme across all sections is the distinction between genetically specified architectural priors and experientially acquired content. Evolution does not install specific social knowledge–it installs the representational format, learning biases, sensitive-period timing, and neurochemical gating that guarantee the right kind of social knowledge will be acquired from the organism’s particular social embedding. The mentalizing network is genetically wired but the specific models of specific people are learned; the attachment system’s neurochemistry is innate but IWM content depends on caregiver behavior; the norm-learning architecture is species-universal but norm content is culturally transmitted; the status-tracking circuitry is phylogenetically ancient but the dimensions of status valued in a given ecology are culturally shaped. This format-content distinction is the key to understanding both the universality of human social cognition (same architecture everywhere) and its cultural variability (different content installed by different social environments) without retreating to either nativist or blank-slate extremes.
